## Objectives

- Follow an email from sender to mailbox: programs, protocols, ports.
- Find the mail servers and policies of a domain with `dig`.
- Tell the **envelope** from the **message**, and see why spoofing is
  easy.
- Use a mock server, and send an email by hand with `ncat`.
- Read a small Java SMTP client.

# A quick reminder about networking

## IP addresses

- Each machine on the Internet has an **IP address**.
- IPv4 (`193.134.223.20`): 32 bits, not enough for every device.
- **NAT**: a router shares one public address between several
  machines, like your home router.
- **IPv6** (`2001:db8::1`): 128 bits, made to solve the shortage.

## Names and the DNS

- The **DNS** translates names into addresses (and more).

```sh
nslookup heig-vd.ch
```

```{.text .fragment}
Non-authoritative answer:
Name:   heig-vd.ch
Address: 193.134.223.20
```

- Your browser does this lookup before it connects.

## DNS records

| Type | Gives |
|---|---|
| `A`, `AAAA` | An IPv4, IPv6 address |
| `CNAME` | An alias |
| `NS` | The DNS servers of the domain |
| `MX` | The servers that receive the mail of the domain |
| `TXT` | Free text, used for policies such as SPF |

## Ports and programs

- **IP address** = street address; **port** = apartment number: one
  program on the machine. 16 bits, 0 to 65535.
- TCP and UDP each have their own ports: TCP port 53 and UDP port 53
  are two different ports.

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em"}
| Range | Examples |
|---|---|
| 0-1023, system | 21 FTP · 22 SSH · 25, 465, 587 SMTP · 53 DNS · 80, 443 HTTP(S) · 110, 995 POP3 · 143, 993 IMAP |
| 1024-49151, registered | 3306 MySQL · 5432 PostgreSQL · 6379 Redis · 8080 HTTP · 25565 Minecraft |
| 49152-65535, dynamic | Never registered: temporary connections, private services (51820 WireGuard) |
: {tbl-colwidths="[28,72]"}
:::

# Electronic messaging protocols

## Who is who

- **MUA**, Mail User Agent: the mail program of a person
  (Thunderbird, Outlook, Gmail).
- **MSA**, Mail Submission Agent: accepts the mails of its own users,
  usually after login.
- **MTA**, Mail Transfer Agent: carries mails from server to server, to
  the domain of the recipient.
- **Mailbox**: stores the mails until the MUA fetches them.
- MSA and MTA are often the same server program, with two roles.

## How an email travels

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    B["Bob's MUA"] -- "SMTP, 587 or 465" --> MSA["Bob's server<br>(MSA, then MTA)"]
    MSA -- "MX of gmail.com?" --> DNS[(DNS)]
    MSA -- "SMTP, 25" --> MTA["Alice's server<br>(MTA, mailbox)"]
    MTA -- "IMAP or POP3" --> A["Alice's MUA"]
```

## SMTP sends, IMAP and POP3 read

- **SMTP** pushes a mail one step further, up to the mailbox.
- **POP3** downloads the mails, can delete them on the server.
- **IMAP** keeps them on the server and **synchronizes** the devices:
  read on the phone, read on the laptop.
- A webmail is a MUA running on the server: your browser speaks HTTP,
  the webmail often IMAP.

## Mail ports

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
| Protocol | Use | Plain text | TLS from the start |
|---|---|---|---|
| SMTP | Relay between MTAs | 25 | |
| SMTP | Submission by a MUA | 587, then `STARTTLS` | 465 |
| POP3 | Reading | 110 | 995 |
| IMAP | Reading | 143 | 993 |
:::

- 587: clear text, then `STARTTLS` switches to TLS before anything
  private. 465, 995, 993: TLS at once.
- So ncat can talk to 25 and 587 only.

# DNS records related to email

## Where does the mail of a domain go?

```sh
dig +short heig-vd.ch MX
```

```{.text .fragment}
0 heigvd-ch01b.mail.protection.outlook.com.
```

- Microsoft's servers receive the mail of HEIG-VD.
- `0`: the **preference**. With several MX records, the lowest number
  is tried first.

# Security concerns and spam

## Envelope and message

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Envelope**: SMTP commands, for the servers.

- `MAIL FROM:<...>`: the return path, for error reports.
- `RCPT TO:<...>`: one per recipient. Delivery follows these, never
  `To:` or `Cc:`.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Message**: after `DATA`, for the reader (RFC 5322).

```text
From: Alice <alice@example.com>
To: Bob <bob@example.com>
Subject: Hello from ncat

Hi Bob,
this mail was typed by hand.
```

Headers, an **empty line**, the body.
:::
::::

## Nothing checks that they match

- Servers deliver to the **envelope**, the MUA displays the
  **headers**.
- `From:` can show **any** address: **spoofing**.
- SMTP checks neither `From:` nor `MAIL FROM`.

## A policy against spoofing

- SMTP of 1982: no login, no encryption, any server can claim any
  domain.
- **SPF**, added later: a `TXT` record in the DNS lists the IP
  addresses allowed to send mail for the domain of `MAIL FROM`.
- The receiving server checks it: accept, reject, or spam folder.
- DKIM and DMARC complete it (*Go further*).

## SPF of HEIG-VD

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em"}
```text
v=spf1 ip4:193.134.218.124 ip4:145.232.233.54 ip4:185.144.39.35/32
  ip4:185.144.39.39/32 include:spf.protection.outlook.com
  include:spf.hefr.ch include:_spf.createsend.com
  include:c2qslai37u.powerspf.com -all
```
:::

- `ip4:...` gives an address allowed to send.
- `include:...` allows the addresses of another domain's SPF record too.
- `-all` makes every other address fail (`~all`: accept, but mark as
  suspect).

Spammers on your server: your IP on **blocklists**. Most companies
and schools let Microsoft or Google run their mail.

## Mock servers

- Never test a mail program against a real server: a bug in a loop
  sends thousands of mails to real people.
- A **mock server** speaks the same protocol, delivers nothing, and
  shows what it received.
- **Mailpit**: SMTP on port 1025, web interface on 8025.

```yaml
services:
  mailpit:
    image: axllent/mailpit:v1.32
    ports:
      - 1025:1025
      - 8025:8025
```

## Watching the server

```sh
docker compose logs -f
```

```{.text .fragment}
mailpit-1 | ... msg="[smtpd] starting on [::]:1025 (no encryption)"
mailpit-1 | ... msg="[smtpd] response (192.168.65.1) 503 5.5.1
            Bad sequence of commands (MAIL required before RCPT)"
```

- `-f` follows the log as new lines come; `Ctrl` + `C` stops
  following, Mailpit keeps running.
- Mailpit logs each **error** it answers, not the mails it accepts
  (those are in the web interface).

# A focus on the SMTP protocol

## The commands at each step

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Bob's MUA
    participant S1 as Bob's server
    participant S2 as Alice's server
    participant A as Alice's MUA
    B->>S1: EHLO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO
    B->>S1: DATA, message, QUIT
    Note over S1: stores, finds MX
    S1->>S2: EHLO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO
    S1->>S2: DATA, message, QUIT
    Note over S2: stores in mailbox
    A->>S2: fetch (IMAP or POP3)
```

## The commands

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em"}
| Command | Meaning | Success |
|---|---|---|
| (connection) | The server speaks first | `220` |
| `EHLO <name>` | Hello; the answer lists the extensions | `250`, several lines |
| `MAIL FROM:<address>` | Starts a mail, gives the return path | `250` |
| `RCPT TO:<address>` | One recipient; repeat for each | `250` |
| `DATA` | The message follows | `354` |
| message, then `.` | Ends with a line holding a single `.` | `250` |
| `QUIT` | Goodbye; the server closes | `221` |
:::

## Reading the replies

- **First digit**: `2` success, `3` go on, `4` try again later, `5`
  permanent failure.
- `250-` announces more lines; `250 ` is the last one.
- `2.1.0`: enhanced status code, more detail.
- Command in the wrong place: an error, the connection stays open
  (and Mailpit's log shows it).

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em"}
```text
C: RCPT TO:<bob@example.com>
S: 503 5.5.1 Bad sequence of commands (MAIL required before RCPT)
```
:::

# ncat

## ncat

Opens a TCP connection, sends what you type, prints what it receives.
The protocol is you.

```sh
# Client
ncat -C localhost 1025

# Server: listen on 2525, print what the client sends
ncat -l -C 2525
```

- `-C`: each line ends with `\r\n`, as SMTP requires.
- Install: `sudo apt install ncat` (Ubuntu, WSL), `brew install nmap`
  (macOS).
- Alternatives: `nc`, `telnet` (check their CR LF option).

## Why `-C` matters

- Without `-C`, the terminal sends `\n` alone.
- Mailpit accepts commands ending with `\n`...
- ...but the end of the mail must be exactly `\r\n.\r\n`.
- Without `-C`, the `.` is one more line of text: the server waits
  until its timeout (5 minutes in Mailpit).

## Sending an email by hand

::: {style="font-size: 0.6em"}
```text
S: 220 a825881dcf8e Mailpit ESMTP Service ready
C: EHLO my-laptop.local
S: 250-a825881dcf8e greets my-laptop.local
S: 250-SIZE 52428800
S: 250-ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES
S: 250-8BITMIME
S: 250 SMTPUTF8
C: MAIL FROM:<alice@example.com>
S: 250 2.1.0 Ok
C: RCPT TO:<bob@example.com>
S: 250 2.1.5 Ok
C: DATA
S: 354 Start mail input; end with <CR><LF>.<CR><LF>
C: From: Alice <alice@example.com>
C: To: Bob <bob@example.com>
C: Subject: Hello from ncat
C:
C: Hi Bob,
C: this mail was typed by hand.
C: .
S: 250 2.0.0 Ok: queued as 0WN74Fza0O8ED2H17pjg9l
C: QUIT
S: 221 2.0.0 a825881dcf8e Mailpit ESMTP Service closing transmission channel
```
:::

## A Java SMTP client

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em"}
```java
try (Socket socket = new Socket(host, port);
    BufferedReader in = new BufferedReader(
        new InputStreamReader(socket.getInputStream(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
    BufferedWriter out = new BufferedWriter(
        new OutputStreamWriter(socket.getOutputStream(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8))) {

  expect(in, 220);                  // the server speaks first
  send(out, "EHLO my-laptop.local");
  expect(in, 250);
  send(out, "MAIL FROM:<alice@example.com>");
  expect(in, 250);
  // ...
```
:::

- A `Socket` is a TCP connection with two streams. Around them: the
  readers and writers of chapter 04.

## `send` and `expect`

::: {style="font-size: 0.75em"}
```java
private static void send(BufferedWriter out, String line) throws IOException {
  out.write(line + "\r\n");
  out.flush();
}

private static void expect(BufferedReader in, int code) throws IOException {
  String line;
  do {
    line = in.readLine();
    if (line == null) throw new IOException("The server closed the connection");
  } while (line.length() > 3 && line.charAt(3) == '-');
  if (!line.startsWith(code + "")) throw new IOException("Expected " + code + ", received: " + line);
}
```
:::

- `\r\n` written by hand: `newLine()` writes `\n` on Linux and macOS.
- Without `flush()`, the command stays in the buffer: both sides wait, until a
  timeout.
- Read the **whole** reply, or every next answer is one step late.

## Summary

- MUA, MSA, MTA: SMTP to send (587/465, then 25), IMAP or POP3 to read.
- `MX` says where the mail of a domain goes; SPF fights spoofing.
- The **envelope** decides delivery, the **headers** what the reader
  sees.
- Test against a **mock server**, never a real one.
- ncat: you are the protocol. `-C` for CR LF.
